questions.question: Set out the six steps for building a circuit from a diagram, the order in which a non-working circuit is troubleshot, and the safety rules for low-voltage bench work.
questions.expected_answer: Read the diagram fully, finding the supply and its voltage, counting components, identifying those with polarity, tracing every loop and checking that no line bypasses a component; gather the components and check each rating against the supply; lay them out on the bench in the diagram's arrangement with the supply on the left; connect one lead at a time with the switch open, following the loop from positive to negative and observing polarity for cells, LED and buzzer; trace the built circuit against the diagram, check for bare ends that could touch, then close the switch; observe and record what happens. Troubleshoot from most to least common: complete path with clips on metal, terminals tight, lamp screwed in and switch closing; a live supply tested on a known good lamp; correct polarity of LED, buzzer and cells; a sound component by substitution; and a short indicated by warmth or a lead across a component. Safety: connect with the switch open and keep bare ends apart because a shorted cell burns, disconnect anything that warms, keep hair, sleeves and fingers clear of motor shafts, avoid trailing leads, disconnect and remove cells at the end, and never use mains on the bench.

questions.question: Describe what each of the four card circuits demonstrates, compare two lamps connected in series with two in parallel, and explain how a switch in the main line differs from a switch in a branch.
questions.expected_answer: Battery, toggle switch and lamp in one loop shows the basic torch circuit lighting when closed; battery, push switch and buzzer shows a momentary output that sounds only while pressed and is silent with the buzzer reversed, the basis of a doorbell and a panic button; battery, switch and motor shows the motor running and reversing when its leads are swapped, as a winder lifts and lowers; battery, switch, resistor and LED in series shows the LED lit with its protective resistor and dark when reversed. Two lamps in series share the battery voltage so both are dim and removing one breaks the loop and puts out both, as in old Christmas lights; two lamps in parallel each receive the full voltage so both are at full brightness and removing one leaves the other lit, as in house lighting, while the battery supplies two full currents and runs down faster. A switch in the main line opens the path to every branch and controls all the lamps, while a switch in one branch controls only that branch, as each room has its own switch and the main switch controls all.

questions.question: Explain the follow-the-wire method for drawing a diagram of a built circuit, including how junctions and branches are shown, and describe how the finished diagram is checked and presented.
questions.expected_answer: Begin at the positive terminal of the supply and draw the cell or battery on the left of a rectangle with positive at the top; follow the first lead to the component or junction it reaches and draw that symbol on the next side; continue component by component round the loop until the lead returns to the negative terminal. Where one lead arrives and two leave, draw a dot for the junction and follow each branch in turn, drawing it as a side path that rejoins the main loop at another dot; physical positions on the bench are ignored because only connections matter. Check by tracing from negative back to positive and counting components and junctions, confirming each is in the correct loop or branch, marking polarity on the cell and LED, labelling values and drawing the switch open, and ideally by having a partner build from the diagram and compare behaviour. Present with a ruler, horizontal and vertical lines, right-angle corners, standard uncrowded symbols, dots only at true junctions, and the circuit's name, date and a line of observation beneath.
